title: Security Foundations — CIA, AAA & Defense in Depth
desc: Before tools and frameworks come the mental models. Learn the CIA triad, the AAA controls (authentication, authorization, audit), and why every secure system is built in layers — not behind a single wall.
content:
Security is the practice of making it expensive to attack and cheap to recover. Every framework, tool, and standard you will meet over the next seven days exists to push those two costs in opposite directions. Before any of that, you need three mental models that show up in every architecture review, every incident retro, and every interview.

🔑
The three models for the day
1) The CIA triad — what we are protecting. 2) The AAA controls — how we enforce it. 3) Defense in depth — why we never rely on one control.

The CIA Triad — What We Protect

Every security goal collapses into one of three properties: Confidentiality (only the right people can read it), Integrity (it has not been tampered with), and Availability (it is there when needed). A control that does not serve at least one of these is decoration.

The CIA triad. Trade-offs between vertices are normal — the question is whether the trade-off is conscious.

Confidentiality

Information is only readable by authorized parties. Encryption at rest (disks, databases, backups), encryption in transit (TLS), and access control (RBAC, file permissions) are the workhorses. A misconfigured S3 bucket, a stolen JWT, or a verbose error page leaking stack traces all break confidentiality.

Integrity

Information cannot be modified — accidentally or maliciously — without detection. The tools are cryptographic hashes (SHA-256), HMACs, digital signatures, and append-only logs. When a payment processor verifies a webhook signature before crediting an account, that is integrity.

Availability

The system serves legitimate requests when needed. Threats include DDoS, ransomware, data corruption, and self-inflicted outages. Controls include redundancy, rate limiting, backups, and graceful degradation. Availability is the leg of the triad most often overlooked when talking about "security," yet it has the highest direct revenue impact.

💡
The trade-offs are real
Confidentiality and availability often pull against each other: the more you encrypt and gatekeep, the more ways a request can fail. Integrity and availability can collide too — strict integrity checks may reject corrupt-but-readable data the business would prefer to serve. Security architecture is about choosing trade-offs deliberately, not maximizing every leg.

Quick check
A teammate proposes returning detailed SQL error messages to the user when a query fails — "so we can debug faster in production." Which leg of the CIA triad does this break, and why?
Show answer
Confidentiality. SQL error messages routinely leak table names, column names, and query structure — exactly the schema knowledge an attacker needs to craft injection payloads. Errors should be logged server-side and a generic message returned to the client. (Verbose error pages are also a textbook example of OWASP A05 — Security Misconfiguration.)

AAA — How We Enforce It

Once you know what you are protecting, you need three controls in order. The order matters: skipping or fudging any of them creates a class of vulnerabilities you will see again and again across the OWASP Top 10.

AAA in order: identify, then permit, then record. Skip a step and the next one becomes meaningless.

Authentication (AuthN) — "Who are you?"

Verify identity. Done with one or more factors: something you know (password), something you have (phone, security key), something you are (biometric). Multi-factor authentication (MFA) mixes factor types — a password + an SMS code is two factors of the same kind ("know" twice if your phone is compromised), so it's weaker than password + hardware key.

Authorization (AuthZ) — "What may you do?"

Now that we know who, decide what. The two dominant models are RBAC (role-based: Admin, Editor, Viewer) and ABAC (attribute-based: rules over user, resource, and context). The single most common failure across OWASP categories is collapsing AuthN and AuthZ into one check — "if logged in, allow" — which is how broken access control becomes the #1 web vulnerability.

Audit / Accountability — "What did you do?"

Record what happened so investigation is possible. Without audit, you may discover a breach but never know its scope. Append-only, signed, and centralized logs (often shipped to a SIEM) are the goal — application logs alone are often deleted by attackers post-compromise.

Mnemonic — AAA
"Identify, then permit, then record."
  • Authentication — proves identity (who)
  • Authorization — grants permission (what)
  • Audit — leaves a trail (when, by whom, on what)

Defense in Depth — Layers, Not Walls

The seductive failure mode in security is to find one strong control and trust it. Castles fell. So do firewalls. The principle of defense in depth says: assume any single control will fail, and arrange the system so an attacker has to defeat several independent controls in sequence.

Defense in depth. The crown jewels (data) sit at the centre. An attacker has to defeat each ring independently.

Each layer mitigates a different class of failure:

  • People & policy — training, phishing-resistant MFA, access reviews, runbooks.
  • Perimeter — WAF, DDoS protection, VPN, internet-facing rate limits.
  • Network — segmentation, micro-segmentation, mTLS between services, egress filtering.
  • Host — EDR, hardened images, patch automation, runtime monitoring.
  • Application — input validation, output encoding, parameterized queries, RBAC.
  • Data — encryption, field-level encryption, tokenization, backups, DLP.

Three More Principles That Show Up Everywhere

Least Privilege

Give the minimum permissions required to do the job, for the minimum time required. An IAM role with s3:* when the service only needs s3:GetObject on one bucket is a failure waiting for a credential leak. Same for human admins, CI tokens, third-party integrations.

Fail Closed

When in doubt, deny. If the authorization service is unreachable, do not default to "allow." Most systems should fail closed for sensitive operations and fail open only where availability genuinely outweighs risk (e.g., read-only public content with cached responses).

Zero Trust

The modern reformulation: stop assuming the inside of the network is safe. Every request — whether from a laptop on a corporate VPN or a microservice in the same cluster — must authenticate and be authorized. We will revisit Zero Trust on Day 5.

Flashcard
A logged-in user changes a URL from /orders/123 to /orders/124 and sees someone else's order. Which AAA control failed?
Click to flip ↻
Answer
Authorization. Authentication worked — the user was identified. The system simply never checked whether order 124 belongs to that user. This is the canonical IDOR (insecure direct object reference) and is OWASP A01 — Broken Access Control.

The Security Mindset

Tools change every five years. Mental models do not. Carry these four habits into every design review:

  1. Assume breach. Design as if the attacker is already inside one component. Limit the blast radius.
  2. Trust nothing implicit. Every input crossing a trust boundary is hostile until proven otherwise.
  3. Make the secure path the easy path. If the safe option requires extra work, developers will route around it. Provide secure defaults and approved libraries.
  4. Measure what matters. If you cannot answer "who accessed this PII in the last 90 days," you have an audit gap, not a feature gap.
🔑
Key takeaways
1) The CIA triad names what we protect; every control should clearly serve at least one leg. 2) AAA is enforced in order: identity, then permission, then record — collapsing AuthN and AuthZ is how IDOR happens. 3) Defense in depth is not redundancy for its own sake — it is independent layers, so a breach in one does not collapse the rest. 4) Least privilege, fail closed, and Zero Trust are not slogans — they are the defaults you should justify not using.
